tasks.q: Which attack do strong passwords protect against most directly?
a: A flood of traffic from a botnet
tasks.fb: A long password takes impossibly long to guess.

tasks.q: Give an example of when a password alone isn't enough.
a: When it has been phished or appears in a data breach
When the computer is switched off
When the screen is too small
When the password is 20 characters long
Intercepted or stolen data being understood
tasks.fb: Encryption is about confidentiality, not access.

tasks.q: A laptop with encrypted storage is stolen. What is the result?
a: The thief has the hardware, but can't read the data without the key
The data is emailed back to the owner
tasks.fb: This is why organisations encrypt every mobile device.

tasks.q: Why does physical security matter for network security?
a: Someone with physical access to a server can bypass many other protections
It stops viruses spreading by email
tasks.fb: A locked door is one of the cheapest and most effective controls.

tasks.q: Which is an example of physical security?
a: A locked server room with keycard access
tasks.fb: Physical security protects the hardware itself.

tasks.q: Why do backups defend against ransomware?
a: The files can be restored instead of paying the ransom
tasks.fb: Backups are recovery, not prevention, and they're vital.

tasks.q: Why should a backup be kept disconnected or off-site?
a: Ransomware can encrypt any backup that is connected
tasks.fb: Connected backups get encrypted along with everything else.

tasks.q: Match each threat to the defence that works best against it.
pairs: Encryption, such as HTTPS and a VPN
tasks.fb: In the bonus Cyber defence game you'll have to make exactly these choices, on a budget.

tasks.q: Why do organisations layer their defences?
a: If one protection fails, others still stand between the attacker and the data
It is required to use Wi-Fi
tasks.fb: This is often called defence in depth.

tasks.q: Which combination best protects against a stolen password?
a: Two-factor authentication, access levels and monitoring
A bigger hard drive and a fast router

tasks.q: Is each measure a technical, physical or people-based protection?
items: Keycard access to the IT office
An acceptable use policy everyone signs
CCTV covering the server room door
tasks.fb: A good security plan uses all three types, which is what the Cyber defence game asks you to balance.

info.title: Change it only when needed
info.text: Modern advice is to stop forcing regular password changes: it pushes people towards weak, predictable patterns. Change passwords when there's a reason.

info.title: Encryption by default
info.text: Messaging apps like WhatsApp and Signal use end-to-end encryption, so even the company running the service can't read the messages.

info.title: The cleaner test
info.text: Security teams ask: could someone dressed as a cleaner walk in and plug something into a server? Often the answer used to be yes.

info.title: Test your backups
info.text: A backup that has never been restored isn't a backup. Organisations practise restoring, so they know it works before they need it.

info.title: Patch Tuesday
info.text: Microsoft releases security patches on the second Tuesday of each month. Attackers study them to work out what to exploit on unpatched systems.

info.title: Cheapest first
info.text: Many of the strongest protections, like updates, backups, training and locking doors, cost very little compared with the damage they prevent.
